title: Adding: the resultant and the equilibrant

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the needle on the ring drop to zero as the dashed equilibrant closes the nose-to-tail chain, when you tap "equilibrant".
interactive.title: Forces on a ring
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A small ring sits on the left, pulled by two ropes, and later by three. Each rope's pull is an arrow from the ring, and you drag its nose to change it. Beside the ring the same arrows are laid nose to tail: the second starts where the first ends. The resultant is drawn from the first tail to the last nose, the gap the chain leaves. A needle on the ring points along the net pull, and its length and a readout give its size. The needle works by parts: it adds all the across parts, then all the up parts, then takes Pythagoras on the two sums. A button adds the equilibrant, a dashed arrow from the last nose back to the first tail. It is the resultant turned round, so the chain closes and the needle drops to zero. The screens: two 3 kN pulls with an angle slider from 0° to 180°, reading 6, 4.24, 3 and 0 kN at 0°, 90°, 120° and 180°. A puzzle on the two pulls at 90°. Pulls A and B, 4i + 1j and 1i + 3j kN, added by parts. A puzzle adding 2i + 3j and 4i − 1j. A switch drawing B first, then both orders, to show the parallelogram. A puzzle picking the drawing that shows a + b. The equilibrant of A and B. A puzzle on the equilibrant of 6i − 2j. Three 3 kN pulls 120° apart, closing a triangle. A puzzle on 5 kN east, 5 kN west and 2 kN north. Two mixed puzzles: two 3 kN pulls at 120°, and the third line that holds a ring pulled by 6i + 2j and 2i − 2j kN. Some screens show an idea, and the rest ask you to try it. Each puzzle offers three answers, and a wrong pick is drawn so you can see where it goes wrong.
interactive.ignores: The ring is treated as a single point, so every pull acts at the same place. Pulls on a larger body that act at different points can also turn it, That turning effect is called a moment, and it needs another kind of product. The ropes are drawn straight and weightless. Everything here lies flat on the page. Pulls in 3-D add the same way, with their k parts added too. The puzzles use example values, rounded to two decimal places.

explain.text:
Vectors add nose to tail. Draw the second arrow starting where the first one ends. The arrow from the first tail to the last nose is the sum, called the [[resultant]].[^1] It is the gap the chain leaves, not the chain's length. That is why you cannot add vectors by adding their sizes.[^2] Take two 3 kN pulls on a ring. Pointing the same way, their chain is one straight line, so they make 6 kN. At 90° apart the chain bends, and the gap shrinks to √(3² + 3²) = 4.24 kN. At 120° apart the chain's corner is 60°, so its triangle has three equal sides and the gap is 3 kN. Pulling opposite ways, the second arrow comes straight back, so the gap is nothing. Sizes add only when the pulls point the same way.

Drawing shows the answer, and parts give it exactly. Each arrow is its own parts laid nose to tail. So a chain of arrows is a chain of across parts and up parts. Their order does not change where the chain ends, so you can gather all the across parts together. Lying on one line, they add as plain numbers, and so do the up parts.[^4] Take pull A, 4i + 1j kN, and pull B, 1i + 3j kN. Across, 4 + 1 = 5. Up, 1 + 3 = 4. The resultant is 5i + 4j, and Pythagoras gives its size, √(5² + 4²) = 6.40 kN. The sizes alone would add to 7.28 kN. Draw B first and A second and you reach the same nose, because the parts add to the same sums in either order. The two chains make a parallelogram, and the resultant is its diagonal from the shared tail.

Any gap left in the chain is a net pull, and a net pull sets the ring moving. To hold it still, the pulls must add to nothing. So it needs one more pull that cancels the resultant. That pull is the [[equilibrant]]. It has the same size as the resultant and points the opposite way.[^3] For A and B it is −5i − 4j, also 6.40 kN. Add it to the chain and the last nose lands back on the first tail. The gap is gone, so the net pull is zero. Three pulls in balance close into a triangle, the [[triangle of forces]]. More pulls close into a polygon. Opposite ropes cancel only along their own line. Pulls of 5 kN east, 5 kN west and 2 kN north leave 2 kN north.

**Vectors add nose to tail or part by part to give the resultant, and the equilibrant is the equal and opposite pull that closes the chain.**[^3]

analogy.text: Think of a ring final circuit. The cable leaves the consumer unit, runs round the rooms and comes back to the same terminals. Lay its legs nose to tail and the chain closes, however long it is. The chain ends where it began, so its legs add to nothing, just as balanced pulls do. Stop the run halfway and the straight line back to the board is the gap, much shorter than the cable you used.
analogy.breaks: A cable's legs are laid one after another along a real route. Pulls on a ring all act at once on one point. The nose-to-tail chain is only a drawing that adds them, and its length means nothing.

practice.text:
- Draw every pull as an arrow from the point it acts on.
- Resolve each one into i and j parts, giving each part its sign.
- Add all the i parts. Then add all the j parts. That pair is the resultant.
- Find its size by Pythagoras on those two sums, and its angle by the tangent, with the quarter check from the signs.
- Sketch the chain nose to tail. The gap should point the way your parts say.
- For the equilibrant, flip both signs. It has the same size and points the opposite way.

**Rule of thumb:** Sizes add only when the pulls point the same way. Otherwise the resultant is shorter than the sizes added.

**Worked example:** Say three lines pull on a ring: 2i + 1j, 3i − 4j and −1i + 6j kN. Across, 2 + 3 − 1 = 4. Up, 1 − 4 + 6 = 3. The resultant is 4i + 3j, with size √(4² + 3²) = 5 kN. Its angle is tan⁻¹(3 ÷ 4) = 36.87° above the x-axis. Both parts are plus, so that is the right quarter. The equilibrant is −4i − 3j, 5 kN at 216.87°. The three sizes, 2.24, 5 and 6.08 kN, would add to 13.32 kN.

**Common mistakes**
- Adding the sizes. Two 3 kN pulls at 120° make 3 kN, not 6 kN.
- Using Pythagoras on arrows that are not at right angles. For the 120° pulls it gives 4.24 kN, the answer for 90°.
- Thinking opposite ropes cancel everything. They cancel only along their own line.
- Joining the noses of two arrows drawn from one point. That line is not the sum. The sum is the diagonal from their shared tail.
- Drawing the gap backwards, from the last nose to the first tail. That arrow is the equilibrant.
- Flipping only one sign for the equilibrant.
- Working the parts but never drawing the chain. A sketch catches a sign slip.
